name: Scottish Gaelic
about: Gàidhlig (GAH-lik) is the Gaelic of Scotland, spoken most in the Western Isles, Skye and the west Highlands.
It grew from the same old Gaelic as Irish, but the two have long gone their own ways: cousins, not twins.
The 2022 census counted about 130,000 people in Scotland with some Gaelic, and it is still a home language in the islands.
The Gaelic Language (Scotland) Act 2005 made it an official language of Scotland. There is Gaelic in Nova Scotia, Canada, too.

lessons.title: Halò! Hello and thanks
intro: Halò! You'll hear more Gaelic in the Western Isles than anywhere else in Scotland.
Ten words and you can get through a day here. Well, a morning.

words.note: The ch is the one in 'loch', never the one in 'church'.
To a friend. To an elder, a stranger or a crowd: tapadh leibh (TAH-puh layv).
Gaelic has no single word for yes. You answer with the verb: is it? It is.

lessons.tip: Gaelic has two words for 'you': thu for one friend, sibh for an elder, a stranger or more than one. Leat and leibh follow the same rule.

lessons.title: A h-aon, a dhà: counting
intro: Darts. You'll want to count. In Gaelic, or I'm not letting you near the board.
lessons.tip: Counting out loud, each number takes a little 'a' in front, and the vowel ones gain an h-: a h-aon, a h-ochd.

lessons.title: Beinn is tràigh: island places and weather
intro: Half the map of Scotland is Gaelic once you can read it.
And the other half is weather. Let's do both.

words.note: Ben Nevis is Beinn Nibheis.
Cut in spring, dried on the moor, burnt all winter.
Weather is 'she' in Gaelic: tha i, she is.
Rarer than the word for rain. Use it while you can.

lessons.title: Tì is aran: food and creatures
intro: A Gaelic menu and a Gaelic field guide are mostly the same list, if you're a seal.
lessons.tip: 'Is' between two words is short for agus, 'and': tì is aran, tea and bread.

lessons.title: Mo chù: lenition and liking
intro: Gaelic softens the start of a word after certain little words. It's called lenition.
You write it with an h after the first letter. Cù, a dog. Mo chù, my dog.

words.note: Cù gains an h after mo, 'my', and the c goes soft, like 'loch'.
His softens the word.
Her doesn't. The only clue to whose dog it is.
Glè, 'very', softens: math becomes mhath.
Is toil leam tì: I like tea.
Word for word: Gaelic is at me. Add 'beagan', a little, to be honest.

lessons.tip: Lenition adds an h: c becomes ch, m becomes mh (said 'v'), b becomes bh (also 'v'). That's why it's madainn mhath, not madainn math.

lessons.title: Inbhir and srath: names and borrowings
intro: You've been speaking Gaelic for years. Whisky, slogan, galore.
And every Inver and Strath on the map is Gaelic too.

words.note: Inbhir Nis, Inverness: the mouth of the Ness.
Srath Spè, Strathspey, the valley of the Spey.
Dùn Èideann is Edinburgh.
Kinloch is Ceann Loch, the head of the loch.
Ardnamurchan is Àird nam Murchan.
English kept the first word and wore it down to 'whisky'.
A clan's rallying shout, before it sold toothpaste.

words.english: a visit, a night of songs (ceilidh)
words.note: First a neighbourly visit with songs and stories; the dances came later.

lessons.tip: Irish has the same borrowings from its side: galore comes from gu leòr in Gaelic and go leor in Irish. Cousins, again.

lessons.title: Mas e do thoil e: please, sorry and names
intro: Back for more? Good. Hello and thanks get you a scone. These get you a second one.
And one of them gets you out of trouble, which in a small town is worth more.

words.note: To a friend. To an elder, a stranger or a crowd: mas e ur toil e (mass eh oor TOL eh).
Word for word: take my excuse.
The polite one is 's e ur beatha.

words.local: Dè an t-ainm a th' ort?
words.note: Word for word: what is the name that is on you?
Is mise Ealasaid. Now you.
The most honest sentence in any language. Say it early and often.
Ceud mìle fàilte: a hundred thousand welcomes. We don't do things by halves.
Borrowed from cheerio and kept. The proper goodbye is mar sin leibh.

lessons.tip: Gaelic has a polite 'you' like French vous: sibh. Do thoil and ur toil, leat and leibh, do bheatha and ur beatha all switch with it.

lessons.title: Mo theaghlach: family
intro: Half of Skye is related to the other half. You'll need the words.
Sabhal Mòr Ostaig, down in Sleat, teaches whole degrees in Gaelic. We'll start smaller.

words.note: Mo theaghlach, my family: the t softens after mo.
Sean, old, plus màthair softened: an old mother. Granny.
Sean plus athair.
Mac in a surname is son of: MacLeòid, MacLeod, the son of Leòd.

lessons.tip: Nic is the women's Mac: a MacLeod woman is NicLeòid, the daughter of Leòd. Married or not, the surname stays hers.

lessons.title: Dubh is ruadh: colours and the land
intro: The stones are glas, grey. The moor is donn, brown. The sky does as it likes.
Learn the colours and half the hills on the map tell you what they look like.

words.note: Taigh dubh, the black house of the Harris lesson.
Of hair, foxes and deer. Am Monadh Ruadh, the Cairngorms, is the russet range.
And the green of growing grass. Gaelic cuts the rainbow in different places from English.
Green things that aren't growing: paint, a jumper, a boat.
Of moors, cattle and hair.
Of stone, and of the sea on a dull day.
Am Monadh Liath, the grey hills, face the Cairngorms across the Spey.

lessons.tip: Colours follow the noun, and soften after a feminine one: cù dubh, a black dog, but bò dhubh, a black cow.

lessons.title: Tha an t-acras orm: things that sit on you
intro: In Gaelic you don't have things, they're at you. And you aren't hungry, hunger is on you.
It sounds odd for a week. Then English starts to sound odd.

words.note: Word for word: a dog is at me. Agam, at me.
Is Gaelic at you? Answer tha, or chan eil.
Hunger is on me. Orm, on me.
No money is at me. Say it at the counter and see what happens.

lessons.tip: Agam, agad, aige, aice: at me, at you, at him, at her. Orm, ort, air, oirre: on me, on you, on him, on her. Gaelic bolts the person onto the little word.

lessons.title: An, am, a': the word for the
intro: The museum has six of the Lewis chessmen. I have the word for 'the'. Mine changes shape more.
Four ways to say it, and each one tells you whether the word is a he or a she.

words.note: The plain form, before most consonants.
Am before b, f, m and p: am baile, am fear.
A masculine word starting with a vowel takes t-.
Beinn is feminine, so 'the' softens it.
Feminine too.
Feminine, but d and t never soften after 'the'.
Tha an t-uisge ann: the water is in it. It's raining.
Feminine with a vowel: plain an, no t-.
Feminine s takes a t- in front and falls silent.
Gaelic puts 'the' on its own name. Feminine, so it softens.

lessons.tip: Masculine: an, am, and an t- before a vowel. Feminine: a' with softening, an before d, t and vowels, an t- before s. Learn each noun with its 'the' and you get its gender free.

lessons.title: Cill, achadh, druim: more map words
intro: Every second Highland village is a Gaelic sentence that English has sat on.
Kil, Auch, Drum, Knock. Once you have them, a road sign reads like a story.

words.note: Cille Mhoire, Kilmuir on Skye: Mary's church.
Achadh na Sìne, Achnasheen: the field of the storm, on the road to Kyle.
Druim na Drochaid, Drumnadrochit: the ridge of the bridge, on Loch Ness.
Said with an r: cn turns to cr in the mouth.
Hundreds of Craigs on the map, and a good few people.
Caol Loch Aillse, Kyle of Lochalsh: the narrows of Loch Alsh.
An Tairbeart on Harris, and more besides: anywhere two lochs nearly meet.
Taigh an Droma, Tyndrum: the house on the ridge.
Am Monadh Ruadh and Am Monadh Liath, either side of the Spey.
Kil- on a map is sometimes this, not cill. The map won't tell you which.

lessons.tip: Dalwhinnie, Drumochter, Aviemore: Dail Chuinnidh, Druim Uachdair, An Aghaidh Mhòr. Say the Gaelic and the English spelling suddenly makes sense.

lessons.title: Òran is seanfhacal: songs, the Mòd and sayings
intro: An Comunn Gàidhealach was founded here in Oban in 1891, and the first Mòd sang here the year after.
So this is the right pub for the songs. Most of them are.

words.note: Òran luaidh, a waulking song: the beat of the tweed on the table.

words.english: a gathering; the Mòd, the Gaelic festival
words.note: The Royal National Mòd moves town each October: choirs, poetry, pipes, and a gold medal for solo song.
Bàrd was Gaelic before it was English.
A woman watches the sea for her boatman. Everybody knows the chorus and nobody knows all the verses.
Word for word: my ruin.
Alba is Scotland. Gu bràth: till the end of time.

words.local: Is fheàrr Gàidhlig bhriste na Gàidhlig sa chiste
words.english: Broken Gaelic beats Gaelic in the coffin
words.say: iss SHAHR GAH-lik VREESH-tchuh nuh GAH-lik suh CHEESH-tchuh
words.note: A saying. So say it badly: it still counts.

lessons.tip: Suas leis a' Ghàidhlig! Up with Gaelic! An Comunn Gàidhealach's motto, and the only slogan you'll hear at a Mòd.
